card.title: A tank with a rubber sheet

body.question: What does a capacitor do?
options: It stores electrical energy by holding charge on two insulated surfaces
body.reveal: A capacitor stores energy by accumulating electric charges on two closely spaced surfaces that are insulated from each other. In the water picture it is a flexible diaphragm in a pipe: charge moves on both sides while no electrons actually pass through. The earliest ones were Leyden jars in the 1740s.

probes.question: In the water-pipe analogy, a capacitor is like...
options: A flexible diaphragm sealed in a pipe

probes.question: True or false: in a capacitor, electrons actually pass through the dielectric.

image_brief.show: File:Paper Capacitor from RIFA.jpg and File:Dubilier S635 mica capacitor, 1940s (01).jpg show capacitors

claims.claim: Capacitor stores electrical energy by accumulating charge on two closely spaced insulated surfaces
claims.quote: stores electrical energy by accumulating electric charges on two closely spaced surfaces that are insulated from each other

claims.claim: Water picture: flexible diaphragm sealed in a pipe (probe 1)
claims.quote: a flexible diaphragm sealed inside a pipe

claims.claim: Tank with a rubber sheet dividing it
claims.quote: A capacitor is equivalent to a tank with one connection at each end and a rubber sheet dividing the tank in two lengthwise

claims.claim: No electrons pass through the dielectric (probe 2 false)
claims.quote: No current actually flows through a perfect dielectric
claims.note: Page says 'perfect dielectric'; card states it without 'ideal'. Acceptable for the ideal capacitor model; wording 'in an ideal capacitor' would be exact.

claims.claim: Earliest capacitors were Leyden jars in the 1740s
claims.quote: when European experimenters discovered that electric charge could be stored in water-filled glass jars that came to be known as Leyden jars
